# HTML

For HTML the extension adds an index of its own at the end of the body, or at
your placement marker if the document has one: an
unnumbered level-one heading — **Index**, or your document language's word for
it where the extension covers that language — in a section whose id is `qi-index`
where the document has not taken that name and a minted one where it has (see
below), listed in the table of contents, followed by a nested bullet list of
the entries. It is built out of Pandoc's own document nodes rather than out
of HTML text, so Pandoc's writer does the escaping. No stylesheet is added; the
class names below are hooks for styling it yourself.

Each mark that contributes a locator needs somewhere for its locator to link
to:

- a mark carrying an id of your own keeps it, as long as nothing else on the
  page carries that same name, and the index links to that id;
- every other mark gets an anchor on its own span — `qi-mark-1`, `qi-mark-2`
  and so on, numbered in the order the marks are written.

In a book, a chapter read back from [its own source](books.qmd) rather than
from a record is the one place the first rule is not settled against a rendered
page: that route never sees one, so it links to the id you wrote whether or not
something else on the page carries that name. A mark in a book chapter's front
matter is a second exception — it links to the chapter's page either way, and
it keeps whatever id you wrote on it, contested or not, with nothing reported:
the filter cannot see which of the title-block fields Quarto prints, so it
cannot tell whether that name reaches the page at all. A mark this filter
cannot index at all is the third — one with no visible text and no `entry=`,
which it reports as unindexable and then leaves exactly as you wrote it, id and
all. Such a mark keeps a contested name, so the name stays on two elements and
nothing further is said about it; its id is still moved out of a heading, which
is the one thing that would put it on the page twice on its own.

Where something else on the page does carry that name, the mark gives it up:
one id names one element, and a name on two of them sends every link to
whichever one the browser picks. The element you wrote the name on keeps it —
the extension renames nothing of yours but its own mark spans — and the mark is
given a minted id instead, which for a mark that files a locator is where that
locator then points. Between two marks written with one name, the one whose
locator links to the name keeps it, whichever you wrote first; between two of a
kind the first in the document keeps it and the rest yield. A mark that only
points at another entry has no locator to move, but it carries an id like any
other span and gives a contested one up the same way. Each yield is reported as
the render runs, naming the id given up and what the mark files under — the
term it prints, or the entry you wrote for it — so nothing moves out from under
a link of your own in silence.

An id counts where it is an attribute of an opening tag, and nowhere else. One
written inside an HTML comment is on nothing the rendered page carries, so it
contests nothing: a mark written with that name keeps it. So is one written on
a closing tag, whose attributes a browser reads and drops — `</p id="mine">`
puts `mine` on nothing at all. And so is one written in the text content of
`script`, `style`, `xmp`, `iframe`, `noembed`, `noframes` or `textarea`: a
browser reads those seven elements' content as text rather than as markup, and
so does this reading, which steps over that text and goes on with the markup
after it. A name on a real element standing after one of the seven, in that
same raw HTML block, is counted like any other.

`title` is the one element of that kind this rule does not cover: an `id=`
written in a document title's own text is read as markup and counted, so a mark
written with that name yields it to a carrier the page does not have.

One kind of name is missed by that reading, and a mark written with it keeps it
whatever else carries it, with nothing reported: a name Quarto's own writer
makes up after this extension has run — a footnote's `fn1`, a code block's
`cb1`, `title-block-header` — does not exist yet when the reading is taken, so
writing one of those on a mark still leaves it on two elements.

A heading is the one place an anchor cannot sit, because Quarto copies a
heading's contents into the sidebar table of contents, and an id in there
would end up in the page twice. So a heading mark's anchor — your own id or a
minted one — is placed on an invisible element just after the heading, and
the locator lands at the start of that section. Such a mark is numbered where
its anchor lands; a mark inside a footnote written in that same heading keeps
its anchor with the footnote's text and numbers ahead of it.

Each entry carries an id too, `qi-entry-1` onward, so that a cross-reference
can link to it. Both kinds of generated id skip any name an element of the
rendered page carries — written as an attribute of your own element, or in raw
HTML in your source — so writing `qi-mark-1` yourself is safe: the numbering
steps over it and your element keeps the name. That leaves gaps in the
sequence, which is harmless — the numbers are link targets, not a count of
anything. The section id is minted the same way: `qi-index` where the name is
free, and `qi-index-1`, `qi-index-2` and so on where the document has taken it.
Two kinds of name sit outside that promise. An id injected around the document
at render time is never seen by the filter (`include-in-header` and its
relatives). And a name written where the page renders no element — inside an
HTML comment, on a closing tag, or in the text content of one of the seven
elements above — is a name the numbering may mint: nothing of yours is displaced by that, there being no
element of yours to displace.

An entry's locators are numbered links to those anchors: `1`, `2`, `3` for the
first, second and third time the term is marked, restarting at `1` for each
entry. So `pandoc, 1, 2, 3` in an HTML index means what three page numbers mean
in a printed one. The pieces carry these classes:

| Class | On |
|---|---|
| `qi-term` | the entry's own text |
| `qi-locators` | the run of numbered links |
| `qi-xref`, with `qi-see` or `qi-see-also` | one cross-reference |
| `qi-target` | the target text inside a cross-reference |

A document with no marks gets no index section and no anchors.
